analysis.one_liner: Requires defense contractors to give the Pentagon fair access to repair parts, tools, and manuals.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, introduced in September 2025 with 5 cosponsors, has sat in the House Armed Services Committee since the day it was introduced, with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that sell equipment to the Department of Defense to agree in writing to give the Pentagon access to the parts, tools, and repair information needed to fix that equipment — at the same prices and terms the companies offer their own authorized repair shops. It would let agencies waive the rule for older programs with a documented technical risk assessment, and it directs a review of existing contracts to strip out intellectual property limits that stop military mechanics from doing their own repairs.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and military maintenance crews, who could get equipment diagnosed and fixed faster without waiting on the manufacturer or an authorized dealer. Taxpayers benefit too, since the Pentagon would no longer have to pay monopoly prices for parts and repair services, and any independent repair contractors working for the military would gain access to the same materials as authorized shops.

how_it_helps.text: Defense agencies could not sign a procurement contract unless the contractor agrees in writing to give the Department of Defense fair and reasonable access to all the parts, tools, and information used to diagnose, maintain, or repair the goods, at prices and terms no worse than what the manufacturer offers its own authorized repair providers.

If a manufacturer does not sell a part or tool to any authorized repair provider, the government would determine a fair and reasonable price itself, preventing companies from using authorized-repair exclusivity to lock out military mechanics.

The Defense Secretary would have to review existing contracts to identify modifications that remove intellectual property constraints limiting the Pentagon's ability to maintain and repair the equipment it already owns.
The Comptroller General would have to report to Congress within a year of enactment on how well the Defense Department is complying with the new repair-access requirement, creating accountability.

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors and original equipment manufacturers, who would lose exclusive control over spare parts, diagnostic tools, and repair manuals for equipment sold to the Pentagon — and the repair revenue and pricing power that comes with it. Some companies might also raise upfront contract prices to offset lost aftermarket margins.

drawbacks.text: Contractors could respond by raising the prices they charge on new equipment bids to make up for lost parts and repair revenue, meaning some of the savings could show up as higher upfront procurement costs.

The bill lets agency heads waive the requirement for any program that began before enactment, so the Pentagon's large existing fleets — where repair lock-in problems are already baked in — could escape the rule with only a written justification to Congress.
The bill applies only to Defense Department purchases; it would do nothing for farmers, hospitals, or consumers who face the same manufacturer repair restrictions on civilian equipment.
The waiver process and the contract-modification review rely on agency self-policing, and the only outside check is a single Government Accountability Office report due one year after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: contractors keep less control over repair of equipment the government already bought, and the military gets equipment back in service faster at lower cost. The main good-faith objection is that sharing repair materials could raise bid prices or expose sensitive technical data, but the bill addresses the data concern only indirectly through the waiver process, and the waiver carve-out for legacy programs plus the reliance on agency self-review mean the bill's impact would depend heavily on how the Pentagon implements it. It is a narrow, procurement-scoped fix, not a general right-to-repair law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing, markup, or floor action, while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the Warrior Right to Repair Act on September 4, 2025, joined as original cosponsors by Representative Jen Kiggans, a Republican from Virginia, and Representative Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat from New Hampshire.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services the same day and no further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.
The bill has 5 total cosponsors, split between 2 Republicans and 3 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, defense contractors and equipment manufacturers remain the default winners: with the bill parked in committee, they keep exclusive control of the parts, tools, and repair information for equipment the Pentagon has already paid for, and no repair-access requirement has been added to any must-pass defense bill yet.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support is small but genuinely bipartisan: 5 cosponsors split 2 Republicans and 3 Democrats, with a Republican original cosponsor, and no recorded opposition so far.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to House Armed Services die there quietly, and that is the most likely path here unless the repair-access language is folded into the annual National Defense Authorization Act, which is the usual vehicle for procurement reforms like this. The bipartisan sponsorship and the Pentagon's own documented complaints about repair restrictions give it a plausible, if uphill, route into a larger defense bill.
